# Roddi Health

> Roddi Health is a mobile app in development for owners of rats, hamsters, guinea pigs, rabbits, chinchillas, degus, mice and other small pets. It brings medication reminders, symptom and weight logs and vet visit history together in one place, even for several pets. Roddi Health does not replace a veterinary consultation.

Status: in development, with a free early access list. It is free during the beta. Launch date, pricing and platforms are not announced yet.

The project grew out of a rat blog followed by 7,000+ people on Instagram and TikTok (@marchin_rats). Contact: roddihealth@gmail.com

The site is available in Ukrainian (default) and English. Articles are original overviews written from the veterinary sources they name (RSPCA, PDSA, PetMD and similar); they are reference material, not diagnosis or treatment advice.

Short version with links: https://roddihealth.app/llms.txt


# English articles

## Dust baths for chinchillas: why, how often and for how long

URL: https://roddihealth.app/en/blog/chinchillas/chinchilla-dust-baths
Updated: 2026-11-16

Summary: Chinchillas clean themselves in dust, which takes excess oil and moisture out of their dense fur. Bathing them in water is a bad idea: the fur takes a long time to dry and the skin can become inflamed. A bath of special dust is offered for a limited time and then removed so the dust doesn’t irritate the eyes.


### Why chinchillas need dust

A chinchilla’s fur is extremely dense: several dozen hairs grow from a single follicle (PetMD says up to 60, the RSPCA says 60–90). It is an adaptation to cold high mountains. By rolling in dust, a chinchilla removes excess skin oil, dirt and moisture from its coat. PDSA warns that without these baths the fur can become matted. A bath is also enrichment.


### Why not water

Dense fur dries slowly and holds moisture. According to PetMD, this can lead to matting and inflamed skin. That is why chinchillas are not bathed or wetted.


### Which dust to choose
- Use dust or sand made specifically for chinchilla baths. According to PetMD, it is a fine, cleaned powder made from volcanic ash, pumice, kaolin or silver sand.
- Ordinary sand and similar products not meant for chinchillas are too abrasive and can irritate the skin, eyes and airways.
- Extra-fine dust can irritate the nose and eyes, especially in chinchillas under a year old.
- Replace the dust when it gets clumpy.


### The bath bowl

Use an open-top bowl or tray the chinchilla can roll around in freely, such as a shallow metal bowl. A closed box traps moisture. Sources differ on depth: PetMD suggests about 2.5 cm (1 inch), PDSA 4–6 cm.


### How often and how long

SourceHow oftenHow longPetMD, dust bath article2–4 times a week10–30 min; 3–4 min for chinchillas under a yearPetMD, care guideat least a few times a weeknot statedRSPCAdailynot statedPDSAdailyup to 10 min

All sources agree on one thing: the bath does not stay in the cage all the time. Agree the frequency with your vet and watch the condition of the coat and skin. PetMD warns that going more than a week without a bath can lead to excess oil and skin irritation.


### Why the bath is removed

According to PetMD, constant access to dust can cause conjunctivitis and dry skin. Chinchillas may also use the bath as a toilet, so the RSPCA advises removing or sieving the dust after use.


### Room conditions

The RSPCA advises keeping chinchillas indoors in a dry, well-ventilated, draught-free room, ideally at 10–18 °C: heat, humidity and draughts can make them ill. PetMD adds that humidity should stay below 40–50% and the cage should be out of direct sunlight.


### When to see a vet

Take your chinchilla to a vet if you notice bald patches, discharge from the eyes or nose, or wet fur around the eyes or mouth. See our chinchilla health article for other warning signs.

Sources:
- https://www.petmd.com/exotic/care/how-give-your-chinchilla-dust-bath
- https://www.petmd.com/exotic/chinchilla-care-sheet
- https://www.rspca.org.uk/adviceandwelfare/pets/rodents/chinchillas
- https://www.rspca.org.uk/adviceandwelfare/pets/rodents/chinchillas/environment
- https://www.rspca.org.uk/adviceandwelfare/pets/rodents/chinchillas/health
- https://www.pdsa.org.uk/pet-help-and-advice/looking-after-your-pet/small-pets/chinchilla-health

## Chinchilla health: teeth, fur, digestion and warning signs

URL: https://roddihealth.app/en/blog/chinchillas/chinchilla-health
Updated: 2026-11-16

Summary: A chinchilla’s teeth grow throughout life, so the core of its diet is unlimited hay, not sugary mixes. Saliva on the chin, a poorer appetite, weight loss or fewer droppings can mean mouth pain or digestive trouble. Chinchillas hide illness, so these signs are a reason to see a vet straight away.


### Why spotting problems early matters

PetMD notes that chinchillas are good at hiding illness, so dental problems can go unnoticed until they are severe. PDSA and the RSPCA recommend checking your chinchilla every day, and the RSPCA also advises a vet check-up at least once a year.


### Teeth

A chinchilla’s teeth grow continuously and wear down through chewing. That is why the core of the diet is hay and grass, and PetMD advises unlimited good-quality hay. Pellets are given sparingly, without sugary treats. PDSA advises avoiding muesli-style mixes: chinchillas pick out the sugary bits, which can lead to painful dental disease. Chew blocks or untreated apple or pear branches are good for gnawing.

Signs of dental problems, according to PetMD:
- drooling and wet fur on the chin
- eating less, dropping food, pawing at the mouth
- weight loss and fewer droppings
- swelling of the jaw or face
- overgrown or crooked front teeth
- less grooming and lethargy

In a 2001 UK study (Crossley), dental changes were found on external examination in 35% of chinchillas that looked healthy. The author also noted that jaw swelling, weight loss or changes in chewing occur with various dental problems, so a vet has to find the actual cause. According to PetMD, examining the back teeth usually needs sedation and X-rays, and teeth must never be trimmed at home. If pain stops a chinchilla eating, gut stasis or infection can develop and become life-threatening within hours or days.


### Digestion

The RSPCA advises checking every day that your chinchilla eats and leaves plenty of dry droppings. If eating or drinking habits change, or droppings decrease or stop, contact a vet straight away: the chinchilla may be seriously ill. Diarrhoea and soft droppings are also a reason for a visit.


### Fur and skin

Fur loss can be a sign of illness or injury. The RSPCA also lists chewing its own or others’ fur, and patches of fur coming away when the chinchilla is handled, as signs of stress. Fur release is a defence response that can happen with rough handling. Without dust baths the fur becomes matted; we cover them in a separate article.


### Heat and humidity

Dense fur is an adaptation to cold, so heat and humidity are dangerous for chinchillas. Sources give slightly different ranges: the RSPCA recommends 10–18 °C in a dry, draught-free room, while PetMD gives roughly 13–21 °C, never above 27 °C, with humidity below 40–50% and no direct sun.


### Daily check
- Eyes and nose free of discharge, fur around the eyes and mouth dry.
- The chinchilla eats and drinks, and droppings are normal and plentiful.
- No bald patches, no skin changes.
- No sore or injured feet, no limping.
- No unusual swellings.
- Stable weight: PetMD advises monitoring body weight.

Sources:
- https://www.pdsa.org.uk/pet-help-and-advice/looking-after-your-pet/small-pets/chinchilla-health
- https://www.rspca.org.uk/adviceandwelfare/pets/rodents/chinchillas/health
- https://www.rspca.org.uk/adviceandwelfare/pets/rodents/chinchillas/environment
- https://www.petmd.com/exotic/conditions/mouth/overgrown-chinchilla-teeth
- https://www.petmd.com/exotic/chinchilla-care-sheet
- https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1748-5827.2001.tb01977.x

## Degus at home: housing, company, diet and health

URL: https://roddihealth.app/en/blog/degus/degus-at-home
Updated: 2026-11-16

Summary: Degus are active by day and live in groups, so they are not kept alone. They need a tall metal cage with several levels and a wheel, deep bedding for digging and dust baths a few times a week. The core of the diet is hay, with a few sugar-free pellets, because degus are prone to diabetes.


### Lifestyle and company

Degus are active by day and very vocal. They are social animals: the RSPCA warns that alone they can become depressed and advises keeping a single degu only on a vet’s advice. Keep single-sex groups or a neutered male with females, with no more than one male in a mixed group. PetMD advises against housing degus with other rodents or rabbits. Sources give different lifespans: PDSA says 6–8 years, sometimes 9; the RSPCA 6–7 years; PetMD 5–9 years.


### The cage
- The cage must be metal: degus chew through plastic and wood. PetMD advises avoiding plastic cages and accessories.
- Size: PDSA advises as large a cage as possible, and PetMD gives a minimum of about 71 × 46 × 71 cm for two degus, with bars no more than 1.3 cm apart.
- A tall cage with several levels and solid shelves and floor. A solid roof helps degus feel safe.
- Pear, apple or beech branches for climbing and gnawing.
- A nest box with hay for sleeping.
- Glass tanks are not suitable: the RSPCA links them to breathing problems.
- Keep the cage indoors, out of draughts and direct sun, away from the TV and music: vibration frightens them.


### Heat

The RSPCA advises keeping the room with the cage no warmer than 20 °C and placing it away from radiators. A degu lying flat on its stomach may be overheating: contact a vet straight away.


### Exercise and digging

A solid wheel is needed, big enough for the degu to run with a straight back. PetMD gives a diameter of 25–30 cm. PDSA advises letting degus out for at least half an hour a day into a safe room or pen with wires and wood covered. For digging they need a deep layer of hay and shredded paper. Sources disagree on wood shavings: the RSPCA allows non-toxic shavings, while PetMD advises against them because of the risk to breathing.


### Dust baths

SourceHow oftenHowPDSAa few times a weekchinchilla or hamster sand, not left in all the time because it dries the skinRSPCA2–3 times a week, about 20 min eacha heavy bowl with about 4 cm of sand, removed after usePetMDabout twice a weekchinchilla dust, outside the cage


### Diet
- The core is unlimited hay.
- Degu pellets: PDSA and PetMD suggest one to two tablespoons a day. If degu pellets are not available, guinea pig or chinchilla pellets without molasses will do.
- The RSPCA considers rabbit, hamster and gerbil food, and mixes with dried fruit, unsuitable.
- Leafy greens and vegetables in small portions: PDSA suggests once or twice a week, PetMD a few times a week.
- PetMD advises no fruit, honey, molasses or seeds at all. PDSA allows an occasional bit of apple. The RSPCA allows carrot, sweet potato and beetroot only in tiny pieces now and then.
- Be careful with shop-bought treats: they are often too sugary.
- Degus eat some of their own droppings: this is normal.
- Introduce new food gradually.


### Diabetes

According to the RSPCA and PDSA, degus are prone to type 2 diabetes, especially on a diet high in carbohydrates and sugar. PDSA lists these signs: cloudy eyes (cataracts), drinking a lot and urinating often, and weight gain. If you notice any of these, see a vet.


### Teeth

Degus’ teeth grow continuously and wear down as they chew hay. The RSPCA says healthy teeth are yellow-orange, white teeth can be a sign of illness, and advises checking them every week. According to PDSA, dental problems can show as drooling, a swollen face, discharge from the eyes and a change in tooth colour. Only a vet should correct overgrown teeth.


### The tail and handling

Never pick up or pull a degu by the tail. The skin on the tip of the tail can come off, and then a vet is needed because of the risk of infection. The RSPCA advises letting the degu climb onto your palm and lifting it in cupped hands, low over the floor. Hands swooping down from above frighten them.


### Health checks

The RSPCA advises checking degus every day. A healthy degu has bright, clear eyes, clean ears, a glossy coat, and a clean tail and rear end. Warning signs include nasal discharge, wetness around the mouth, cloudy eyes and white teeth. Take your degus to a vet at least once a year. PetMD advises seeing a vet urgently if a degu eats less, loses weight, breathes with difficulty, has diarrhoea, struggles to chew or becomes lethargic.

Sources:
- https://www.rspca.org.uk/adviceandwelfare/pets/rodents/degus
- https://www.rspca.org.uk/adviceandwelfare/pets/rodents/degus/environment
- https://www.rspca.org.uk/adviceandwelfare/pets/rodents/degus/diet
- https://www.rspca.org.uk/adviceandwelfare/pets/rodents/degus/health
- https://www.rspca.org.uk/adviceandwelfare/pets/rodents/degus/company
- https://www.rspca.org.uk/adviceandwelfare/pets/rodents/degus/behaviour
- https://pdsa.org.uk/pet-help-and-advice/looking-after-your-pet/small-pets/ideal-environment-for-degus
- https://www.petmd.com/exotic/care/caring-for-a-degu

## What to feed a degu: hay, pellets and go easy on sugar

URL: https://roddihealth.app/en/blog/degus/what-to-feed-a-degu
Updated: 2026-11-16

Summary: The basis of a degu’s diet is unlimited good-quality hay. Pellets are given in small amounts and without molasses, because degus are prone to diabetes. Fruit and starchy vegetables are best limited or left out.


### What the diet is based on

Most of the diet is hay, available at all times, such as timothy or meadow hay. Hay wears down the continuously growing teeth and supports the gut. Exotic Direct advises against brown or green hay, because green hay can cause bloating, and says a pink or white coating means mould.

Degu pellets are given in limited amounts: PDSA suggests one to two tablespoons, about 10 g a day, and PetMD one to two tablespoons depending on size and activity. If degu pellets aren’t available, guinea pig or chinchilla pellets without molasses will do. The RSPCA considers rabbit, hamster and gerbil food, and mixes with dried fruit, unsuitable.


### Vegetables and fruit

PDSA suggests a small portion of leafy greens and vegetables once or twice a week, no more. The RSPCA and PetMD advise against fruit because of its sugar, while PDSA allows an occasional bit of apple. Introduce new foods gradually.

FoodWhat sources sayCabbage, broccoli, fresh herbsExotic Direct: once or twice a week; cabbage and broccoli can cause bloatingApple, cucumberExotic Direct: once a month. PDSA: an occasional bit of apple. PetMD and the RSPCA advise no fruitCarrot, sweet potato, beetroot, parsnipRSPCA: only tiny pieces now and then. Exotic Direct: carrot once a monthPeas, cornExotic Direct: once a month. PetMD: avoid as starchyPotatoesPetMD: avoidSugary rodent chews, food with molasses, human leftoversPDSA: don’t give

Sources disagree, so if in doubt follow the stricter option and talk to your vet.


### Diabetes

Degus are prone to type 2 diabetes, especially on a diet high in sugar and carbohydrates. PDSA and Exotic Direct list these signs: drinking and urinating more, cloudy eyes (cataracts), and, according to PDSA, weight gain. If you notice them, see a vet.


### Water and vitamin C

Change the water daily, as PDSA and Exotic Direct advise. Exotic Direct advises against adding vitamin C to the water, because you can’t control how much the degu drinks and the vitamin breaks down quickly. If needed, it can come from food such as broccoli or red pepper.

Sources:
- https://www.rspca.org.uk/adviceandwelfare/pets/rodents/degus/diet
- https://pdsa.org.uk/pet-help-and-advice/looking-after-your-pet/small-pets/ideal-environment-for-degus

## Basic guinea pig care: hay, food, housing and company

URL: https://roddihealth.app/en/blog/guinea-pigs/guinea-pig-care-basics
Updated: 2026-11-16

Summary: The core of a guinea pig’s diet is unlimited hay and grass. On top of that come a few guinea pig pellets, fresh vegetables every day and clean water. Guinea pigs are social and live in pairs or groups. They need a roomy home with a solid floor, hides and space to move.


### Hay and grass

Hay should make up most of the diet and be available at all times. PDSA puts its share at 85–90%, PetMD at about 80%. The RSPCA advises giving fresh grass as often as possible, ideally daily. Lawnmower clippings are dangerous and must not be fed.


### Pellets

Choose uniform pellets made for guinea pigs, grass-based, rather than muesli-style mixes. PDSA suggests about one tablespoon per adult guinea pig a day; the RSPCA says a portion following the manufacturer’s instructions, fresh each day.


### Vegetables and fruit

PDSA suggests about a cup of vegetables per guinea pig a day, 5–6 different kinds, including some rich in vitamin C. Among foods that can be given often, the RSPCA lists bell peppers, cucumber, celery, romaine lettuce and parsley, while broccoli, spinach, kale, carrot and a quarter of an apple are treats for a few times a week. Fruit is given rarely because of its sugar. Introduce new foods gradually.

Don’t give iceberg lettuce, potato, onion, garlic, mushrooms, avocado, rhubarb, chocolate, bread and biscuits, nuts or grains.


### Water

Fresh, clean water must always be available. The RSPCA advises checking it twice a day and making sure it doesn’t freeze in winter. Wash the bowl or bottle every day.


### Housing

Sources give different minimum sizes:

SourceMinimumPetMDa cage of about 91 × 76 × 46 cmPDSAa hutch of at least 1.5 × 1 m and a run of at least 2 × 1 mRSPCA Australiaat least 2 × 0.5 m for a pair, at least 30 cm high

All agree that bigger is better. The floor should be solid, not mesh. The RSPCA advises having one more hide than there are guinea pigs, and giving them space to move every day. PetMD suggests at least an hour a day outside the cage.


### Temperature

The RSPCA gives 17–20 °C as a comfortable room temperature. Above 26 °C the risk of heatstroke rises, and below 15 °C a guinea pig can get chilled. PDSA warns of heatstroke above 27 °C. Keep the home away from radiators, sunny windows and draughts.


### Bedding and cleaning

Dust-free hay or paper bedding works well; cotton wool should not be used. Sources disagree about wood shavings, so paper bedding is the safer choice. Remove wet bedding and leftover fresh food every day, and do a thorough clean once a week.


### Company

The RSPCA advises keeping a guinea pig with at least one friendly companion unless a vet advises otherwise. Good pairings are a neutered male with one or more females, two females, or brothers raised together. A male living with females must be neutered: according to PDSA, females can become pregnant from about three weeks old. A rabbit is not a companion for a guinea pig, and keeping them together is not advised.


### Health checks
- Check your guinea pig every day: face and eyes, coat, rear end and feet.
- Check the front teeth and nails once a week. Overgrown teeth must be corrected by a vet.
- In hot weather check the rear end twice a day: soiled fur attracts flies.
- Take your guinea pig to a vet at least once a year.
- If eating, drinking or droppings change, or droppings stop, contact a vet straight away. Difficulty breathing is an emergency.

Sources:
- https://www.rspca.org.uk/adviceandwelfare/pets/rodents/guineapigs

- https://www.rspca.org.uk/adviceandwelfare/pets/rodents/guineapigs/environment
- https://www.rspca.org.uk/adviceandwelfare/pets/rodents/guineapigs/company
- https://www.rspca.org.uk/adviceandwelfare/pets/rodents/guineapigs/health
- https://www.pdsa.org.uk/pet-help-and-advice/looking-after-your-pet/small-pets/guinea-pigs-as-pets
- https://www.pdsa.org.uk/pet-help-and-advice/looking-after-your-pet/small-pets/your-guinea-pig-s-diet
- https://www.pdsa.org.uk/pet-help-and-advice/looking-after-your-pet/small-pets/the-ideal-home-for-your-guinea-pig
- https://www.pdsa.org.uk/pet-help-and-advice/looking-after-your-pet/small-pets/guinea-pig-health

## Guinea pig not eating: what to do

URL: https://roddihealth.app/en/blog/guinea-pigs/guinea-pig-not-eating
Updated: 2026-11-16

Summary: If your guinea pig has stopped eating or is producing fewer droppings, call a vet straight away. According to PetMD, untreated gut stasis can become fatal within 24–48 hours.


### Why it is so dangerous

A guinea pig’s gut has to keep moving all the time, and for that it needs a lot of fibre. When the gut slows down, gas builds up and the balance of gut bacteria is upset, and the condition gets worse quickly. PetMD calls stasis a life-threatening emergency. On top of that, according to PDSA and the RSPCA, guinea pigs hide illness, so by the time you notice a guinea pig isn’t eating the problem may have started earlier.


### Possible causes

According to PetMD, stasis is often the result of another problem:
- too little hay and fibre
- dehydration
- pain or illness, including dental problems
- stress: a new place, handling, changes in companions
- too little exercise

PDSA adds that changing food too quickly can also upset digestion and make a guinea pig stop eating. A vet finds the cause: the exam usually covers the teeth, weight, belly and X-rays, and in severe cases blood tests.


### What to do now
- Call a vet as soon as possible: PetMD and the RSPCA advise contacting one straight away.
- Note when the guinea pig last ate and passed droppings.
- If you can, bring a droppings sample.
- Don’t give medicines without a prescription: the RSPCA advises only those a vet has recommended.

According to PetMD, treatment usually includes fluids, assisted feeding and pain relief. Many guinea pigs start improving within 24–72 hours and fully recover within several days to a week.


### Which droppings are normal

Guinea pigs eat special soft droppings straight from their bottom, and this is a normal part of digestion. What should worry you is different: the RSPCA advises contacting a vet immediately if droppings become fewer, stop, become softer than usual or stick to the fur.


### How to lower the risk
- Hay and clean water available at all times. The RSPCA advises checking the water twice a day.
- Daily exercise: PetMD suggests at least an hour a day outside the cage.
- Introduce new food gradually.
- Weigh your guinea pig regularly: according to PDSA, weight loss can be a sign of illness.
- Check the front teeth and rear end every day.
- See a vet at the first change in appetite.

Sources:
- https://www.petmd.com/exotic/gi-stasis-in-guinea-pigs
- https://www.rspca.org.uk/adviceandwelfare/pets/rodents/guineapigs/health
- https://www.rspca.org.uk/adviceandwelfare/pets/rodents/guineapigs/diet
- https://www.pdsa.org.uk/pet-help-and-advice/looking-after-your-pet/small-pets/guinea-pig-health
- https://www.pdsa.org.uk/pet-help-and-advice/looking-after-your-pet/small-pets/your-guinea-pig-s-diet
- https://www.petmd.com/exotic/guinea-pig-care-sheet

## Scurvy in guinea pigs: signs of vitamin C deficiency and prevention

URL: https://roddihealth.app/en/blog/guinea-pigs/guinea-pig-scurvy
Updated: 2026-11-16

Summary: Guinea pigs can’t make vitamin C themselves, so they need it from food every day. According to PetMD, signs of deficiency can appear after just 2–3 weeks of a poor diet: the coat, appetite and weight get worse, wounds heal slowly and moving becomes painful. A vet finds the cause and prescribes treatment.


### Why vitamin C must come from food

Unlike most animals, guinea pigs lack the enzyme needed to make vitamin C, so they get it only from food. Vitamin C is needed, among other things, to make collagen. PDSA warns that without it a guinea pig is at risk of scurvy.


### How a deficiency shows

PetMD, in an article written by a vet, lists these signs:
- a rough, dull or patchy coat
- lethargy and a depressed look
- poor appetite and weight loss, or poor weight gain in young animals
- wounds heal slowly and infections become more frequent
- dental problems and pain when chewing
- diarrhoea
- bone and joint pain, swollen joints: the guinea pig is reluctant to move or limps

In severe cases a deficiency can lead to fractures, paralysis, sepsis and death. Many of these signs also occur with other diseases, so a vet has to find the cause.


### How quickly it happens

According to PetMD, signs can appear after just 2–3 weeks of a diet that is too low in vitamin C. The most common reasons are too little fresh produce, no fortified food, or food and treats that are too old.


### Fresh vegetables every day

The RSPCA calls fresh vegetables and herbs an excellent source of vitamin C. Among foods that can be given often, it lists bell peppers, cucumber, celery, romaine lettuce and parsley. PetMD lists red and green peppers, broccoli, cauliflower, strawberries and kiwi among foods rich in vitamin C.

Sources disagree about high-calcium greens. The RSPCA gives kale and spinach only as treats a few times a week. PetMD’s care sheet advises avoiding parsley, spinach, kale and dandelion because of the risk of stones, while PetMD’s vitamin C article lists kale and parsley as good sources. If in doubt, ask your vet.


### Pellets lose vitamin C
- Choose pellets made for guinea pigs, grass-based and fortified with vitamin C.
- Vitamin C in food breaks down over time, faster with heat, light and air.
- PDSA advises storing pellets somewhere dry, cool and dark and using them within three months of purchase. According to PetMD’s care sheet, vitamin C levels drop sharply three months after the production date.
- The RSPCA advises giving a fresh portion of pellets daily instead of topping up the old one, and not feeding food past its best-before date.


### Vitamin C in water and supplements

Vitamin C in drinking water is unreliable: it breaks down quickly, and PetMD says such additives last less than a day. PDSA advises against adding it to water also because the taste can make a guinea pig drink less.

According to PDSA, a guinea pig that gets a balanced diet with fresh greens every day does not need separate supplements. Too much vitamin C can also do harm: Improve International, a publisher for vets, links excessive amounts with urinary stones and joint problems. So it is worth discussing supplements with your vet.


### What a vet will do

According to PetMD, the vet examines the guinea pig and asks about its diet, and sometimes takes X-rays or a blood test. Correcting the diet is often enough, and in severe cases the vet prescribes vitamin C. Dental changes can last a long time.

Sources:
- https://www.petmd.com/exotic/conditions/cardiovascular/c_ex_gp_vitamin_c_deficiency
- https://www.petmd.com/exotic/guinea-pig-care-sheet
- https://www.pdsa.org.uk/pet-help-and-advice/looking-after-your-pet/small-pets/your-guinea-pig-s-diet
- https://www.rspca.org.uk/adviceandwelfare/pets/rodents/guineapigs/diet
- https://www.rspca.org.uk/adviceandwelfare/pets/rodents/guineapigs/health
- https://improveinternational.com/uk/clinical-library/guinea-pigs-and-the-vitamin-c-problem

## What to feed a guinea pig and where to get vitamin C

URL: https://roddihealth.app/en/blog/guinea-pigs/what-to-feed-a-guinea-pig
Updated: 2026-11-16

Summary: Hay and grass make up most of a guinea pig’s diet and must always be available: PetMD puts their share at about 80%, PDSA at 85–90%. Guinea pigs can’t make vitamin C themselves, so they get it from food every day, above all from fresh vegetables.


### Hay and grass

Hay must always be available. RSPCA Australia suggests a daily pile of hay twice the size of the guinea pig. Almost any grass hay is suitable. Sources disagree about alfalfa: PetMD advises avoiding it because regular eating can cause harm, while RSPCA Australia allows it for young, pregnant, nursing and ill guinea pigs, and only occasionally for others. Fresh grass is good, but lawnmower clippings must never be fed.


### Pellets

Pellets are given in limited amounts: PDSA suggests about a tablespoon per adult guinea pig a day. Choose grass-based pellets fortified with vitamin C and check they are fresh, because the vitamin breaks down over time. Sources define the limit differently: PDSA says three months after purchase, PetMD’s care sheet three months after production, the RSPCA by the best-before date.


### Vegetables and fruit

Fresh vegetables are given every day, but sources give different amounts: PDSA suggests about a cup per guinea pig, PetMD a quarter to half a cup. Fruit is where they disagree most: SPCA New Zealand recommends plenty of fresh fruit and vegetables daily, PetMD fruit once or twice a week, PDSA fruit as a treat once every week or two. Introduce new food gradually: PDSA suggests changing the diet over two to four weeks.


### Where to get vitamin C

Guinea pigs can’t make vitamin C, so they need it every day. SPCA New Zealand considers pellets and vitamin C in drinking water unreliable sources because it breaks down quickly, and recommends fresh vegetables. The RSPCA and PDSA treat fortified pellets as a source. PDSA adds that a supplement may help if you’re unsure your guinea pig gets enough, but it shouldn’t be added to water. See our scurvy article for the signs of deficiency.


### Greens high in calcium

SPCA New Zealand recommends leafy greens such as kale, parsley and spinach for vitamin C. PetMD’s care sheet warns that these are high in calcium, and guinea pigs are prone to bladder stones. The RSPCA allows parsley often and kale and spinach as treats. Ask your vet how much of these greens suits your guinea pig.


### What not to give

FoodWho advises avoiding itIceberg lettuce, potato, garlic, avocadoRSPCA, PDSAOnion, mushrooms, chivesPDSA, PetMDRhubarbPDSAChocolate, daffodils, buttercups, liliesPetMDBread, biscuits, cakes, grains, seeds, nutsPetMD, RSPCA AustraliaCitrus, coconutRSPCALawnmower clippingsRSPCA, PDSA, RSPCA Australia

Sources disagree about peas, beans and corn: PetMD counts them as starchy foods to avoid, while RSPCA Australia lists them among vegetables that can be fed.


### Water

Fresh water must always be available. The RSPCA advises checking it twice a day and making sure it doesn’t freeze in winter. PetMD advises changing bowl water daily.

Sources:
- https://www.petmd.com/exotic/guinea-pig-care-sheet
- https://spca.nz/advice-and-welfare/article/why-is-vitamin-c-important-for-my-guinea-pigs
- https://www.rspca.org.uk/adviceandwelfare/pets/rodents/guineapigs/diet
- https://www.pdsa.org.uk/pet-help-and-advice/looking-after-your-pet/small-pets/your-guinea-pig-s-diet
- https://kb.rspca.org.au/categories/companion-animals/other-pets/guinea-pigs/what-should-i-feed-my-guinea-pigs
- https://www.petmd.com/exotic/conditions/cardiovascular/c_ex_gp_vitamin_c_deficiency

## A hamster for beginners: answers to common questions

URL: https://roddihealth.app/en/blog/hamsters/hamster-for-beginners
Updated: 2026-11-16

Summary: Syrian hamsters live alone, while dwarf hamsters can sometimes live in pairs if they grew up together. Hamsters need a roomy cage with deep bedding for digging, a solid wheel that keeps their back straight, pelleted food and quiet during the day, as they are active at night.


### Syrian or dwarf?

The RSPCA lists five species commonly kept as pets: Syrian, Chinese, Campbell’s Russian dwarf, winter white dwarf and Roborovski. Syrians are larger: about 13–18 cm long according to PetMD, while dwarfs are 5–10 cm. The species determines the size of the wheel and cage and whether hamsters can live together.


### Can two hamsters live together?

Syrian and Chinese hamsters live alone: they are not naturally social, and Syrians are never housed together. Sources disagree about dwarfs. The RSPCA and PetMD allow pairs or trios if they grew up together, ideally littermates, but warn they may fall out later, so be ready to separate them. PDSA advises against housing Russian dwarfs together. New hamsters are not added to a group.


### Which cage

Sources give different sizes:

SourceMinimumPDSA100 × 50 cm (citing a German veterinary animal welfare association)PetMD, Syrianabout 102 × 51 × 41 cmPetMD, dwarfabout 61 × 30 × 30 cm per hamster

All agree that bigger is better. PDSA prefers a single-level cage to a tall multi-level one. The floor should be solid, not mesh. The RSPCA advises against wooden cages. PetMD gives bar spacing of about 1.3 cm for Syrians and about 0.6 cm for dwarfs.


### Bedding and nest

Hamsters dig, so bedding should be deep. PDSA recommends at least 25 cm, PetMD 15–25 cm for Syrians, and for dwarfs 5 cm across the cage with about 20 cm in one corner. Unscented paper bedding is the safest choice. The RSPCA, PDSA and PetMD advise against cotton wool and fluffy fibres: the threads wrap around feet. Hay, shredded paper and unscented toilet paper work for the nest. Sources disagree about wood shavings and newspaper: PDSA considers shavings too dusty and newspaper ink toxic.


### The wheel

The wheel should be solid, with no gaps or rungs, and big enough to keep the hamster’s back straight: in a small wheel the back arches, which can cause pain over time. Recommended sizes differ:

SourceSyrianDwarfPDSAat least 30 cmat least 20 cmPetMD, Syrian care sheet28–30 cmnot statedPetMD, general care sheetat least 20 cmat least 15 cm

The RSPCA reminds owners that a wheel shouldn’t be the only enrichment.


### Hamsters sleep by day

Hamsters are active at night. Don’t wake them, pick them up while they sleep or clean the cage during the day. A hamster woken suddenly may get scared and bite. Keep the cage somewhere quiet, away from the TV, washing machine and direct sun, and switch the light off at about the same time each evening.


### Temperature

Keep your hamster indoors, away from draughts and damp. PDSA recommends a steady 18–21 °C, PetMD 20–24 °C for Syrians. Heat brings a risk of heatstroke, and in the cold a hamster can go into torpor. If a hamster is cold, limp and barely responsive, PetMD advises seeing a vet straight away.


### What to feed
- The core is pelleted hamster food: every pellet is the same, so a hamster can’t pick out the tasty bits. PDSA suggests muesli-style mixes only as an occasional extra.
- Fresh vegetables and greens in small amounts, one or two teaspoons a day according to PDSA. Too much fresh food can cause diarrhoea.
- Fruit rarely and in tiny portions. PDSA warns that Russian dwarfs are prone to diabetes, so sugary food is especially harmful for them.
- Don’t give grapes, rhubarb, chocolate, caffeine, alcohol, fruit pits and seeds, raw potato, garlic, or sugary and salty food.
- Hamsters hoard food, so remove leftover fresh food the same day, but leave dry food stores in place when cleaning.
- Water must always be available. Check the bottle daily for leaks or blockages.

Sources contradict each other on onion and tomato: PDSA lists them as suitable, while PetMD advises avoiding onions and unripe tomatoes. It is safer not to give them.


### How to pick up a hamster

According to the RSPCA, first let the hamster sniff your hand, then offer two cupped palms so it can climb on by itself. Hold it only a few centimetres above a stable surface: falls from a height are dangerous. Don’t grab or squeeze. Only handle a hamster when it is awake. Children shouldn’t hold a hamster without an adult.


### Cleaning

Remove dirty bedding, droppings and leftover fresh food every day or every few days. Sources disagree about full cleans: PetMD says weekly, PDSA weekly for small cages and every few weeks for larger ones, the RSPCA once or twice a month. Put back a little old, dry bedding so the nest still smells familiar.


### When to see a vet urgently

Hamsters lose condition quickly and hide pain. See a vet straight away if your hamster eats less, has diarrhoea, has wet or dirty fur under the tail (this may be wet tail), loses weight, breathes with difficulty, sneezes, has discharge from the nose or eyes, drools, has overgrown teeth, has cheek pouches that stay swollen for hours, or an eye bulges out.

Sources:
- https://www.rspca.org.uk/adviceandwelfare/pets/rodents/hamsters
- https://www.rspca.org.uk/adviceandwelfare/pets/rodents/hamsters/environment
- https://www.rspca.org.uk/adviceandwelfare/pets/rodents/hamsters/diet
- https://www.rspca.org.uk/adviceandwelfare/pets/rodents/hamsters/behaviour
- https://www.rspca.org.uk/adviceandwelfare/pets/rodents/hamsters/company
- https://www.rspca.org.uk/adviceandwelfare/pets/rodents/hamsters/health
- https://www.pdsa.org.uk/pet-help-and-advice/looking-after-your-pet/small-pets/hamsters-as-pets
- https://www.petmd.com/exotic/hamster-care-sheet
- https://www.petmd.com/exotic/syrian-hamster-care-sheet
- https://www.petmd.com/exotic/dwarf-hamster-care-sheet

## Wet tail in hamsters: symptoms and what to do

URL: https://roddihealth.app/en/blog/hamsters/wet-tail-in-hamsters
Updated: 2026-11-16

Summary: “Wet tail” is diarrhoea that soaks the fur under the tail. A hamster loses fluid quickly, so it is often an emergency: PetMD advises that a vet who treats exotic animals should see the hamster, ideally within 24 hours.


### What it is

The term usually refers to diarrhoea in young hamsters, although it can happen at any age. Fluid loss leaves the hamster dehydrated and weak, it eats less and its coat looks scruffy. PetMD warns that without prompt treatment the hamster can die, and PDSA that death is sometimes sudden.


### Why it happens

According to PetMD, causes can be infectious: bacteria, especially in hamsters 3–10 weeks old, protozoa and intestinal parasites. They can also be non-infectious:
- a sudden change of food or brand
- too many pellets, vegetables, fruit or sweet treats
- stress: transport, heat or high humidity, overcrowding
- a dirty cage and spoiled food in hidden stores
- some antibiotics (PetMD names penicillin) that kill the good bacteria in the gut


### What to do now
- Call a vet who treats exotic animals as soon as possible.
- Don’t give medicines, especially antibiotics, without a prescription: the RSPCA warns that some antibiotics can cause serious digestive problems in hamsters.
- Take a fresh droppings sample and note what you feed, the room temperature and humidity, and whether any new hamsters arrived.
- Handle the hamster less and don’t disturb it more than necessary.
- Some bacteria that cause wet tail can infect people. Wash your hands after contact and ask the vet how to handle the hamster during treatment.

The vet may give fluids, medicines and supportive care. According to PetMD, improvement is often seen within two to three days, and recovery takes one to two weeks or longer. Don’t change the diet during recovery unless the vet advises it.


### How to lower the risk
- A calm home without temperature swings.
- Remove leftover food and dirty bedding every day.
- A balanced diet without sudden changes; store food in an airtight tub or jar.
- Don’t overfeed vegetables and fruit.
- Keep new hamsters apart for at least 30 days, as PetMD advises.

Sources:
- https://www.petmd.com/exotic/condition/wet-tail-in-hamsters
- https://www.pdsa.org.uk/pet-help-and-advice/looking-after-your-pet/small-pets/hamsters-as-pets
- https://www.rspca.org.uk/adviceandwelfare/pets/rodents/hamsters/health
- https://www.rspca.org.uk/adviceandwelfare/pets/rodents/hamsters/diet
- https://www.petmd.com/exotic/hamster-care-sheet

## What to feed a hamster: what’s allowed and what isn’t

URL: https://roddihealth.app/en/blog/hamsters/what-to-feed-a-hamster
Updated: 2026-11-16

Summary: Most of a hamster’s diet should be a pelleted hamster food. Fresh food is given in moderation, because too much of it can cause diarrhoea, which is dangerous for a hamster: it loses fluid quickly.


### What the diet is based on

The basis is a pelleted hamster food. PDSA explains that all pellets are the same, so a hamster can’t pick out the tasty bits, and advises against muesli-style mixes as the only food. PetMD recommends food with 15–25% protein and about a tablespoon of food a day, depending on the species.

Choose high-fibre vegetables and give them in small amounts: PDSA suggests one or two teaspoons of fresh food a day. Hamsters are active at night, so fresh food is best given in the evening. Fruit is high in sugar. For Syrians, PetMD advises apple or berries only rarely and in tiny portions; for dwarfs, a teaspoon of fruit one to three times a week. PDSA warns that Russian dwarf hamsters are prone to diabetes, so they should get especially little sugary food.


### Can hamsters eat it: a quick table

FoodAnswerNoteGrapes, rhubarbNoRSPCA: can be poisonous to rodentsGarlicNoPetMDOnionBetter notPetMD advises avoiding it, while PDSA lists it as suitable. Safer not to giveChocolate, coffee, alcoholNoPetMD: toxicCitrusNoPetMD advises avoiding it; PDSA thinks it’s best avoided for nowAlmondsNoOn PetMD’s list; PDSA allows other nuts as an occasional treatRaw beans, raw potatoNoPetMDTomatoesCarefulPetMD advises avoiding unripe ones, PDSA allows tomatoFruit pits and seedsNoIncluding apple seedsSugary, salty food, red meatNoPetMDApple without seeds, banana, peachIn moderationA small piece; PDSA lists them as suitableCourgette, bell pepper, carrotIn moderationCourgette and pepper are on PDSA’s list, carrot is mentioned by PetMD


### What to watch out for
- A sudden change of food or brand: the RSPCA, PDSA and PetMD warn it can upset the gut and cause diarrhoea.
- Too many vegetables, fruits or sweet treats.
- Spoiled leftovers. Hamsters hoard food, so fresh food goes off quickly in their stores. PetMD advises removing leftovers and hidden fresh food daily, and for Syrians after a few hours.


### Water

Fresh, clean water must always be available. The RSPCA recommends a sipper tube without a ball valve, because hamsters find it hard to drink from ball valves. PetMD advises changing the water daily and checking the bottle for leaks and chew damage.

## Pet mice: housing, cleaning, food and company

URL: https://roddihealth.app/en/blog/mice/pet-mice-care
Updated: 2026-11-16

Summary: Mice are social, nocturnal animals. They need same-sex companions, a roomy, well-ventilated home without draughts, and places to hide and climb. The core of the diet is a pelleted mouse food, with fresh greens within the daily ration and clean water every day.


### Company

Mice are social and should live with other mice. Keep stable single-sex groups. Males are often aggressive towards unfamiliar males, so a male group is best made of brothers who grew up together. Females usually accept newcomers more easily. A male lives with females only if he is neutered. The RSPCA advises keeping a mouse alone only if a vet says so, and not housing other rodents with mice.


### Housing
- Sources give no exact floor area for pet mice. They advise as much space as possible, and PDSA considers most pet-shop cages too small.
- The home needs good airflow without draughts. Ammonia builds up in glass tanks and solid plastic boxes.
- Bar spacing of no more than 5 mm (RSPCA Australia) or 6 mm (PDSA).
- A solid floor: wire mesh hurts their feet.
- Several levels, ladders and ropes: mice are good climbers.
- Several hides with two exits, and a dark spot for a nest.


### Where to put it

PDSA and the New South Wales schools guide give 18–22 °C as a comfortable range, without sudden swings. Keep the cage out of direct sun and draughts, and out of bathrooms, garages and conservatories. Mice need quiet, away from the TV and loud music, as they are sensitive to noise and light. RSPCA Australia suggests 8–12 hours of dark, quiet time a day.


### Bedding and nest

SuitableNot suitablepaper or card bedding, cellulose pelletsfine sawdust, scented or coloured beddingfor the nest: shredded paper, tissues, haycotton wool and fluffy fibres: they tangle around feeta layer of at least 2 cm, with one 3–4 cm area for diggingcorn cobs

Sources disagree about wood shavings: RSPCA Victoria and the New South Wales schools guide allow them, while the RSPCA, PDSA and RSPCA Australia advise against them. Paper bedding is the safer choice.


### Cleaning
- Remove droppings and wet bedding every day.
- PDSA recommends a full clean every week; the RSPCA says every one to two weeks.
- Mice scent-mark their territory. Put back a little dry old bedding so the home still smells familiar.
- Clean in the evening, when mice wake up.
- Check the water bottle morning and evening: mice can block the spout with bedding.


### What to feed
- The core of the diet is mouse pellets or blocks. Each pellet contains everything needed, so a mouse cannot pick out only the tasty bits.
- RSPCA Australia and RSPCA Victoria advise against seed mixes: mice pick their favourite parts, which leads to imbalance and obesity. PDSA allows mixes but suggests switching to pellets if a mouse leaves part of the food.
- Fresh dark greens and non-starchy vegetables in small portions, as part of the daily ration rather than on top of it.
- Treats should be no more than 10% of calories.
- Don’t give chocolate, grapes or raisins, avocado, garlic, onion, coffee, tea, alcohol, sweets, fatty or dairy foods, or sticky food.
- Scatter some food so the mice can forage for it.
- Fresh water every day. RSPCA Australia recommends a drinking bottle, ideally two in case one fails.
- Introduce new food gradually.


### Gnawing and exercise

Mice’s incisors grow throughout life, so they need things to gnaw made of untreated wood or cardboard. A wheel should be solid, with no gaps or rungs, and big enough for the mouse to run with a straight back. The RSPCA reminds owners that a wheel shouldn’t be the only enrichment: add tunnels, boxes and ropes.

Sources:
- https://www.rspca.org.uk/adviceandwelfare/pets/rodents/mice
- https://www.rspca.org.uk/adviceandwelfare/pets/rodents/mice/environment
- https://www.rspca.org.uk/adviceandwelfare/pets/rodents/mice/company
- https://www.pdsa.org.uk/pet-help-and-advice/looking-after-your-pet/small-pets/mouse-health
- https://kb.rspca.org.au/categories/companion-animals/other-pets/rats-and-mice/where-should-i-keep-my-mice
- https://kb.rspca.org.au/categories/companion-animals/other-pets/rats-and-mice/what-should-i-feed-my-mice
- https://rspcavic.org/learn/caring-for-your-mice-and-rats/
- https://education.nsw.gov.au/teaching-and-learning/animals-in-schools/animals-in-schools-species/mice/mice-environment

## How to check a pet mouse’s health: daily check and warning signs

URL: https://roddihealth.app/en/blog/mice/pet-mouse-health-check
Updated: 2026-11-16

Summary: Mice hide illness, so by the time symptoms are obvious a mouse is often already seriously ill. A short check every morning and evening helps you spot changes early: dull eyes, a ruffled coat, unusual breathing, weight loss or a mouse that sits apart from the others.


### Why check every day

Mice can go downhill quickly and show only faint signs of pain until things are severe. RSPCA Australia explains that as prey animals they hide illness: if a mouse looks sick, it is already very sick. Check your mice twice a day, in the morning and evening when they are active. Watch quietly for a few minutes first, then look at each mouse closely.


### What a healthy mouse looks like
- Clear, wide-open eyes.
- A dense, sleek, shiny coat.
- Even, quiet breathing.
- Sleeps curled up in a ball. A mouse lying stretched out may be unwell.
- Moves briskly, eats and sleeps with the others.


### What to look out for

What to checkWarning signsEyesdull or sunken eyes, squinting, dischargeNose and breathingnasal discharge, chattering, fast or laboured breathing with a lot of belly movement, frequent sneezingCoat and skinruffled, dirty or matted fur, droppings stuck under the tail, red skin, bald patchesDroppingsdiarrhoea, soft foul-smelling droppingsWeight and bodyweight loss or rapid weight gain, lumps under the skinBehaviourhiding more than usual, sitting alone in a corner, moving little, losing interest in food, drinking much more

Sources differ slightly on sneezing: the New South Wales schools guide treats any sneezing as a warning sign, while RSPCA Australia suggests seeing a vet if a mouse sneezes more than a few times over an hour or two. Soft droppings vary too. Mice normally eat a special soft dropping, which is healthy, but soft, foul-smelling droppings left in the cage are a concern.


### Why weight matters

The RSPCA notes that losing 20% or more of body weight can be fatal for a mouse. For a 30 g mouse that is just 6 g, so the change is easy to miss by eye. Keeping a weight record helps you see a trend and show it to the vet.


### Common problems
- Respiratory infections. According to RSPCA Australia, they are often caused by Sendai virus and Mycoplasma. Signs: sneezing, chattering, laboured breathing, head tilt, less grooming and weight loss. Treatment eases the symptoms, but the infection and the changes in the lungs remain. Treatment is prescribed by a vet.
- Teeth. Incisors grow throughout life. If they overgrow, the mouse eats less, drools, loses weight and may get a swollen face. A vet trims the teeth, and hard things to gnaw lower the risk.
- Skin and mites. Fur mites are a common cause of skin trouble: thinner, greasy fur on the head and body, and itching. Fur loss without sores can also come from a dominant mouse chewing others’ fur.
- Tumours. The most common cancer in mice is mammary tumours. RSPCA Australia says they can double in size in two weeks or less and are almost always malignant. Show any new lump to a vet straight away.


### New mice and vet visits

The New South Wales schools guide advises keeping new mice apart for four weeks and watching them closely, because they can carry disease without any signs. When you take a mouse to the vet, RSPCA Australia suggests bringing a cage-mate along so they still smell the same afterwards and don’t fall out. Choose a vet who treats mice.

Sources:
- https://www.rspca.org.uk/adviceandwelfare/pets/rodents/mice/health
- https://kb.rspca.org.au/categories/companion-animals/other-pets/rats-and-mice/what-does-an-unhealthy-mouse-look-like
- https://kb.rspca.org.au/knowledge-base/what-are-common-health-problems-in-mice/
- https://education.nsw.gov.au/teaching-and-learning/animals-in-schools/animals-in-schools-species/mice/mice-health
- https://www.pdsa.org.uk/pet-help-and-advice/looking-after-your-pet/small-pets/mouse-health

## Rabbit not eating: why it’s dangerous and what to do

URL: https://roddihealth.app/en/blog/rabbits/rabbit-not-eating
Updated: 2026-11-16

Summary: A rabbit needs to eat and pass droppings all the time. PetMD considers more than 8 hours without food or droppings abnormal, and gut stasis an emergency. The Rabbit Welfare Association advises seeing a vet straight away in that case, without waiting until tomorrow.


### Why it is so dangerous

A rabbit’s digestion depends on food moving through the gut all the time. When it slows down, the balance of gut bacteria is upset and gas and toxins build up. The RSPCA warns that stasis can quickly become life-threatening. PetMD adds that after more than a day without food a rabbit also risks liver damage. A healthy rabbit, according to the Rabbit Welfare Association, produces up to 300 droppings a day, so fewer droppings are a clear warning sign.


### Possible causes

According to Walkerville Vet, the most common cause is gut stasis, but appetite can also go because of:
- dental problems
- kidney disease
- abscesses and pneumonia
- liver lobe torsion
- intestinal blockage

Stasis itself, according to PetMD, can be triggered by anything that causes pain, reduces appetite or dehydrates the rabbit, as well as stress and a low-fibre diet. Walkerville stresses that only a vet can find the cause, and that telling stasis from a blockage is especially tricky.


### How long can you wait

Sources differ slightly: PetMD considers more than 8 hours without eating or passing droppings abnormal, while Walkerville Vet advises seeing a vet if appetite hasn’t improved within 12 hours or the rabbit is quiet. The RSPCA and the Rabbit Welfare Association advise going straight away. The safest choice is the shortest time.


### What to tell the vet
- When the rabbit last ate and last passed droppings.
- What you feed and whether the diet changed.
- Any medicines given recently.
- How its behaviour has changed.
- Whether a female rabbit is spayed.


### What not to do at home
- Don’t massage the belly: Walkerville advises ruling out a blockage first.
- Don’t rely on pineapple, papaya or hairball lubricants. Walkerville says they are usually unnecessary and may even be harmful, and the Rabbit Welfare Association says pineapple won’t help and its sugar may make things worse.
- Don’t give medicines without a vet’s approval.


### How to lower the risk

The RSPCA and the Rabbit Welfare Association recommend a diet of about 85% hay and grass, 10% leafy greens and 5% pellets. Hay must always be available: PetMD warns that rabbits fed only pellets are at higher risk of stasis. Walkerville advises avoiding processed food, fruit, grains, sugar and lucerne hay. The RSPCA also suggests keeping a note of changes in appetite, droppings, behaviour and weight.

Sources:
- https://www.petmd.com/rabbit/conditions/digestive/gastrointestinal-gi-stasis-rabbits
- https://www.walkervillevet.com.au/blog/rabbit-not-eating/
- https://www.rspca.org.uk/adviceandwelfare/pets/rabbits/health
- https://www.rspca.org.uk/adviceandwelfare/pets/rabbits/diet
- https://rabbitwelfare.co.uk/welfare-need/gut-slowdown/

## How to make a rat’s life more interesting: company, play and foraging

URL: https://roddihealth.app/en/blog/rats/enrich-your-rats-life
Updated: 2026-11-16

Summary: Rats are clever, curious and social, so they need at least one companion and new experiences every day. A tall cage with several levels, hides, ropes, digging boxes and food they have to search for help prevent boredom, and time outside the cage should always be supervised.


### Why rats get bored

The RSPCA describes rats as highly intelligent, curious animals with good memories. They learn quickly and need chances to climb, run, forage, explore, play and dig. Without these, a rat gets bored. The RSPCA says chewing the cage bars may signal boredom or a wish to escape, and bald patches from rats chewing each other’s fur may mean they don’t get on or are bored.


### Company

A rat is never kept alone: according to the RSPCA, even plenty of human attention doesn’t replace other rats, and loneliness can lead to depression and abnormal behaviour. Keep pairs or small same-sex groups, ideally siblings. In a mixed group, all males must be neutered. Don’t add or remove rats from a stable group. Keep dogs and cats away: to rats they are predators.


### A cage with plenty to do
- The cage should be large enough for the rat to run, stand on its hind legs, climb and explore. PetMD gives a minimum of about 61 × 61 × 61 cm for one rat and advises the largest home possible. RSPCA Australia notes there is no evidence-based size standard.
- Several levels with ladders and ramps. The RSPCA says levels also reduce squabbles between cage-mates.
- Bar spacing narrow enough that a rat can’t push its head through: about 1.3 cm according to PetMD, up to 2.5 cm for adults according to RSPCA Australia.
- A solid floor: wire mesh hurts feet.
- One more hide than there are rats, with several exits so they can all sleep together.
- Tunnels, natural-fibre ropes, hammocks, ladders. Remove a fabric hammock once it is chewed so the rat doesn’t swallow the fabric.
- Change things around: the RSPCA advises rotating toys regularly.


### Food they have to find

The RSPCA suggests turning feeding into foraging: mix food into the bedding, scatter and hide it, put it in cardboard tubes or egg boxes. Whole foods that take some work, such as a cooled boiled egg in its shell, are good too. This food should come out of the daily ration, not be added to it. Several feeding spots reduce competition.


### Digging and gnawing

For digging, the RSPCA suggests a box of clean sand or compost and a thick layer of bedding in the cage; RSPCA Australia gives 3–4 cm. Rats’ incisors grow throughout life, so they need things to gnaw: wooden chews made for rodents, apple branches, untreated wood.


### Time outside the cage

PetMD says rats need time outside the cage every day. The RSPCA advises letting out only tame, relaxed rats, and only under supervision, in a room they can’t escape from and where they can’t get hurt. Remove cables, toxic plants and anything they could chew. An alternative is a large pen with objects, a digging area and a foraging tray. Sources don’t give a length of time.


### How to train

Rats are very trainable: the RSPCA mentions teaching them to respond to their name or give a high five. Use rewards only and never punish. A useful skill is climbing onto the scales for a treat, which makes weight checks easier. According to the RSPCA, rats are best handled in the morning or evening: let the rat sniff your hand, slide one palm under its body and rest the other lightly over its back. Never lift a rat by the tail or the scruff.


### What to avoid
- Exercise balls: the RSPCA says they restrict exploration and are stressful.
- Scented or coloured bedding, cotton wool and fluffy fibres.
- Strong smells (air fresheners, smoke) and sudden noise, including ultrasound from appliances.
- Glass and solid plastic cages: air doesn’t circulate well.
- Trimming whiskers.


### When boredom may be illness

The RSPCA advises showing a vet any repetitive behaviour, such as constant bar chewing. Signs of stress also include excessive grooming of the head and paws, aggression, red staining around the eyes and nose, hiding and avoiding contact. Rats hide pain, so any change in behaviour is a reason to look more closely.

## How long pet rodents live: rats, hamsters, guinea pigs, degus

URL: https://roddihealth.app/en/blog/rats/how-long-pet-rodents-live
Updated: 2026-11-16

Summary: Mice and hamsters live the shortest, about 1–3 years, rats 2–3 years, guinea pigs 4–8, degus 5–9 years, and chinchillas, according to the RSPCA, 10–20 years. Sources give different figures, so treat these as guides, not exact limits.


### Comparison table

AnimalPetMDRSPCAPDSAMouse18–24 monthsabout 3 years1–3 yearsRatup to 3 years2–3 years2–3 yearsHamster2–3 years (Syrian and dwarf)up to 2 years, some longer2–3 yearsGuinea pigup to 8 years5–6 years4–8 yearsDegu5–9 years6–7 years6–8 years, sometimes 9Chinchillanot compared10–20 yearsnot compared

These are approximate averages with proper care. Sources differ noticeably, especially for mice and guinea pigs, and individual animals live shorter or longer.


### What matters most
- A diet that suits the species, without too much sugar and fat.
- A clean home without strong smells or draughts.
- Companions for social species, exercise and calm handling.
- Regular check-ups: PetMD advises a vet visit for hamsters once a year, and the RSPCA at least once a year for guinea pigs.
- Seeing a vet at the first changes: the RSPCA warns that mice and hamsters lose condition quickly when ill.


### Why keeping records matters

These animals often hide illness, so changes in weight or appetite may be the only early sign. Regular notes help you spot a trend and show it to the vet.

## What to feed a rat: what’s allowed and what isn’t

URL: https://roddihealth.app/en/blog/rats/what-to-feed-a-rat
Updated: 2026-11-16

Summary: The basis of a pet rat’s diet is a pelleted food made specifically for rats. Vegetables, a little fruit, boiled egg, grains and seeds are given within the daily ration, not on top of it. Grapes, raisins, onion and chocolate are not suitable.


### What the diet is based on

Choose pellets made specifically for rats. The RSPCA warns that rabbit, guinea pig or hamster food won’t give rats the nutrients they need. Rats are omnivores, so the diet can be topped up with small amounts of vegetables, fruit, boiled egg, grains and seeds.

These extras come out of the daily portion rather than being added to it. PetMD advises that all extras and treats together make up no more than 10% of the diet: rats gain weight easily. Take the amount of the main food from the instructions on the pack and weigh your rat to keep an eye on its weight.


### Can rats eat it: a quick table

FoodAnswerNoteGrapes, raisinsNoRSPCA, RSPCA AustraliaOnion, garlicNoAll sources name onion; garlic is named by PetMD and RSPCA AustraliaRhubarbNoCitrusBetter notThe RSPCA and PetMD advise avoiding it, while the New South Wales schools guide allows itWalnutsNoOn the RSPCA’s list of harmful foodsChocolate, coffee, tea, alcoholNoPetMD warns that caffeine and alcohol can cause serious illness or deathAvocado, sticky foodNoRSPCA Australia; rats can choke on sticky foodRaw beans, potatoesNoPetMDUnripe tomatoesNoPetMD; ripe ones are not mentioned separatelyFruit pits and seedsNoPetMDDairyBetter avoidFatty; only now and then as a treatGrains, breadA littleSmall amounts of grain; bread is not mentioned separately. RSPCA Australia advises against seed and grain mixes as a foodMost vegetablesYesIn small pieces, within the ration. RSPCA Australia recommends dark greens and non-starchy vegetables


### How to feed
- Twice a day, morning and evening. The RSPCA explains that rats eat mostly at dawn and dusk.
- Scatter some food, mix it into the bedding or hide it in cardboard tubes so the rats forage for it.
- The RSPCA recommends ceramic bowls: metal ones give off ultrasound that bothers rats.
- Remove what hasn’t been eaten. PetMD advises throwing away leftover vegetables and fruit after 10 hours at most.
- Sweet and fatty foods only as an occasional reward during training. PetMD advises avoiding such treats altogether.


### Water

Fresh, clean water must always be available. The RSPCA recommends drinking bottles rather than bowls, several of them, checked twice a day. RSPCA Australia and PetMD advise changing the water daily.

## Why is my rat sneezing, and when to see a vet

URL: https://roddihealth.app/en/blog/rats/why-is-my-rat-sneezing
Updated: 2026-11-16

Summary: Even an occasional sneeze or reddish crusts around the eyes and nose can be the first signs of a respiratory infection. According to RSPCA Australia, it is the most common health problem in rats, and untreated it can turn into pneumonia. So show a sneezing rat to a vet rather than waiting.


### Early signs

At first the symptoms are easy to miss: the rat sneezes now and then, and small reddish crusts appear around the eyes or nose. This is dried red pigment from tears, called porphyrin. Within a few days you may also see:
- frequent sneezing and squinting
- rusty tears or nasal discharge
- poorer appetite and lethargy
- a ruffled coat
- behaviour changes: the rat avoids contact, is irritable or bites

Red staining around the eyes and nose can also come from stress. The RSPCA says a small amount that doesn’t recur is not a worry, while a lot of it can point to a serious problem.


### Why it happens

According to PetMD, most rats naturally carry the bacterium Mycoplasma pulmonis, one of the most common causes of these infections. It passes from rat to rat, and a rat can carry it without any signs. Viruses can also cause disease, and other bacteria join in when immunity is weakened. The New South Wales government schools guide warns that the infection is highly contagious.

The risk rises with age, other illnesses, obesity, stress and overcrowding, ammonia in a dirty cage, and smoke, vaping, scented soap, household chemicals and candles. Pine and cedar bedding irritate the airways, and PDSA warns against any dusty bedding. PetMD considers paper bedding the safer option.


### Why not to wait

PetMD advises that any rat with signs of a respiratory infection should see a vet straight away, and PDSA warns that these infections can get worse very quickly. RSPCA Australia says that once signs are visible, the changes in the lungs are permanent and treatment may be needed for life. PetMD knows of no home remedies that cure the infection, so only give medicines a vet has prescribed.


### While you wait for the appointment
- Clean the cage and remove strong smells nearby.
- Note down when the symptoms started and what has changed.
- You can take a short video of the breathing to show the vet.
- Don’t give medicines or antibiotics without a prescription.


### How to lower the risk
- Keep new rats apart and watch them: PetMD advises at least 2 weeks, the New South Wales schools guide 4 weeks.
- Clean the cage regularly so ammonia doesn’t build up.
- Keep the cage somewhere quiet and clean, well ventilated but free of draughts.

Sources:
- https://www.petmd.com/exotic/conditions/respiratory/upper-respiratory-infection-rats
- https://www.petmd.com/exotic/rat-care-sheet
- https://www.rspca.org.uk/adviceandwelfare/pets/rodents/rats/health
- https://www.rspca.org.uk/adviceandwelfare/pets/rodents/rats/environment
- https://kb.rspca.org.au/categories/companion-animals/other-pets/rats-and-mice/what-are-common-health-problems-in-rats
- https://www.pdsa.org.uk/pet-help-and-advice/looking-after-your-pet/small-pets/rats-as-pets
- https://education.nsw.gov.au/teaching-and-learning/animals-in-schools/animals-in-schools-species/rats/rats-health


# Статті українською

## Чим годувати дегу: сіно, гранули й обережно з цукром

URL: https://roddihealth.app/blog/degu/chym-goduvaty-degu
Updated: 2026-11-16

Summary: Основа раціону дегу — якісне сіно без обмежень. Гранули дають у малій кількості й без меляси, бо дегу схильні до діабету. Фрукти й крохмалисті овочі найкраще обмежити або виключити.


### Основа раціону

Більшу частину раціону становить сіно, яке має бути доступне постійно, наприклад тимофіївка чи лугове. Сіно зношує зуби, що ростуть безперервно, і підтримує кишечник. Exotic Direct радить не давати буре й зелене сіно, бо зелене може спричинити здуття, а рожевий чи білий наліт означає пліснява.

Гранули для дегу дають обмежено: PDSA називає одну-дві столові ложки, тобто близько 10 г на день, PetMD — одну-дві столові ложки залежно від розміру й активності. Якщо гранул для дегу немає, підійдуть гранули для морських свинок чи шиншил без меляси. Корм для кроликів, хомʼяків і піщанок, а також суміші із сухофруктами RSPCA вважає непридатними.


### Овочі й фрукти

PDSA радить невелику порцію листової зелені й овочів один-два рази на тиждень, не частіше. Фрукти через цукор RSPCA і PetMD радять не давати, а PDSA допускає зрідка шматочок яблука. Нові продукти вводьте поступово.

ПродуктЩо кажуть джерелаКапуста, броколі, свіжі травиExotic Direct: один-два рази на тиждень; капуста й броколі можуть спричинити здуттяЯблуко, огірокExotic Direct: раз на місяць. PDSA: зрідка шматочок яблука. PetMD і RSPCA радять фруктів не даватиМорква, батат, буряк, пастернакRSPCA: лише крихітними шматочками зрідка. Exotic Direct: моркву раз на місяцьГорох, кукурудзаExotic Direct: раз на місяць. PetMD: уникати як крохмалистеКартопляPetMD: уникатиСолодкі ласощі для гризунів, корм із мелясою, рештки людської їжіPDSA: не давати

Джерела розходяться, тому за наявності сумнівів дотримуйтесь суворішого варіанту й порадьтеся з ветеринаром.


### Діабет

Дегу схильні до діабету 2 типу, особливо на раціоні з великою кількістю цукру й вуглеводів. PDSA й Exotic Direct називають такі ознаки: дегу більше пʼє й частіше мочиться, очі мутніють (катаракта), за PDSA ще й зайва вага. Із такими ознаками зверніться до ветеринара.


### Вода й вітамін C

Воду міняйте щодня, як радять PDSA й Exotic Direct. Exotic Direct не радить додавати вітамін C у воду, бо неможливо проконтролювати, скільки дегу випʼє, і вітамін швидко руйнується. За потреби він може надходити з їжі, наприклад із броколі чи червоного перцю.

Sources:
- https://www.rspca.org.uk/adviceandwelfare/pets/rodents/degus/diet
- https://pdsa.org.uk/pet-help-and-advice/looking-after-your-pet/small-pets/ideal-environment-for-degus
- https://www.petmd.com/exotic/care/caring-for-a-degu
- https://exoticdirect.co.uk/news/degu-food-advice-what-your-degu-should-be-eating-not-eating-diabetes-and-other-advice/

## Дегу вдома: житло, компанія, раціон і здоровʼя

URL: https://roddihealth.app/blog/degu/degu-vdoma
Updated: 2026-11-16

Summary: Дегу активні вдень і живуть групами, тож поодинці їх не тримають. Їм потрібна висока металева клітка з кількома рівнями й колесом, глибока підстилка для риття й пилові ванни кілька разів на тиждень. Основа раціону — сіно, а гранули дають потроху й без цукру, бо дегу схильні до діабету.


### Спосіб життя й компанія

Дегу активні вдень і дуже балакучі. Це соціальні тварини: RSPCA попереджає, що поодинці вони можуть впадати в депресію, і радить тримати дегу самого лише за порадою ветеринара. Тримають одностатеві групи або кастрованого самця із самками, причому в змішаній групі має бути не більше одного самця. PetMD не радить селити дегу з іншими гризунами чи кроликами. Тривалість життя джерела оцінюють по-різному: PDSA — 6–8 років, іноді 9, RSPCA — 6–7 років, PetMD — 5–9 років.


### Клітка
- Клітка має бути металевою: пластик і дерево дегу прогризають. PetMD радить уникати пластикових кліток і аксесуарів.
- Розмір: PDSA радить якомога більшу клітку, а PetMD для двох дегу називає мінімум приблизно 71 × 46 × 71 см і відстань між прутами не більше 1,3 см.
- Висока клітка з кількома рівнями, полиці й підлога суцільні. Суцільний дах допомагає дегу почуватися в безпеці.
- Гілки груші, яблуні чи бука для лазіння й гризіння.
- Будиночок із сіном для сну.
- Скляні акваріуми не підходять: RSPCA повʼязує їх із проблемами дихання.
- Ставте клітку в приміщенні, без протягів і прямого сонця, подалі від телевізора й музики: вібрація їх лякає.


### Тепло

RSPCA радить, щоб у приміщенні з кліткою було не вище 20 °C, і просить ставити її подалі від батарей. Якщо дегу лежить плазом на животі, вона може перегріватися: одразу звертайтеся до ветеринара.


### Рух і риття

Потрібне суцільне колесо, достатньо велике, щоб дегу бігала з рівною спиною. PetMD називає діаметр 25–30 см. PDSA радить щодня випускати дегу щонайменше на пів години в безпечну кімнату чи вольєр, де закриті дроти й дерево. Для риття потрібен глибокий шар сіна й рваного паперу. Щодо деревної стружки джерела розходяться: RSPCA допускає нетоксичну стружку, PetMD не радить її через ризик для дихання.


### Пилові ванни

ДжерелоЯк частоЯкPDSAкілька разів на тижденьпісок для шиншил чи хомʼяків, не лишати постійно, бо сушить шкіруRSPCA2–3 рази на тиждень, приблизно по 20 хвважка миска з шаром піску близько 4 см, після купання прибратиPetMDприблизно двічі на тижденьпил для шиншил, поза кліткою


### Раціон
- Основа — сіно без обмежень.
- Гранули для дегу: PDSA і PetMD радять одну-дві столові ложки на день. Якщо їх немає, підходять гранули для морських свинок чи шиншил без меляси.
- Корм для кроликів, хомʼяків і піщанок, а також суміші із сухофруктами RSPCA вважає непридатними.
- Листова зелень і овочі — невеликими порціями. PDSA радить один-два рази на тиждень, PetMD — кілька разів на тиждень.
- Фрукти, мед, мелясу й насіння PetMD радить не давати зовсім. PDSA допускає зрідка шматочок яблука. Моркву, батат і буряк RSPCA дозволяє лише крихітними шматочками зрідка.
- Будьте обережні з магазинними ласощами: часто вони надто солодкі.
- Дегу зʼїдають частину свого посліду: це норма.
- Новий корм вводьте поступово.


### Діабет

За RSPCA і PDSA, дегу схильні до діабету 2 типу, особливо якщо в раціоні багато вуглеводів і цукру. PDSA називає такі ознаки: помутніння очей (катаракта), дегу багато пʼє й часто мочиться, набирає зайву вагу. Якщо помітили щось із цього, зверніться до ветеринара. Детальніше про раціон читайте в статті «Чим годувати дегу».


### Зуби

Зуби дегу ростуть безперервно й стираються під час жування сіна. RSPCA пише, що здорові зуби жовто-помаранчеві, а білі можуть бути ознакою хвороби, і радить оглядати їх щотижня. За PDSA, про проблеми із зубами можуть свідчити слинотеча, набряк морди, виділення з очей і зміна кольору зубів. Виправляти зуби, що переросли, може лише ветеринар.


### Хвіст і як брати на руки

Дегу ніколи не беруть і не тягнуть за хвіст. Шкіра з кінчика хвоста може злізти, і тоді потрібен ветеринар, бо є ризик інфекції. RSPCA радить дати дегу самій залізти на долоню й підняти її в складених долонях, низько над підлогою. Руки, що нависають згори, тварину лякають.


### Огляди

RSPCA радить оглядати дегу щодня. У здорової дегу ясні очі, чисті вуха, блискуча шерсть, чистий хвіст і задня частина тіла. Насторожують виділення з носа, волога біля рота, помутніння очей і білі зуби. Щонайменше раз на рік показуйте дегу ветеринару. PetMD радить терміново звертатися до лікаря, якщо дегу гірше їсть, худне, важко дихає, має діарею, погано жує чи стала млявою.

Sources:
- https://www.rspca.org.uk/adviceandwelfare/pets/rodents/degus
- https://www.rspca.org.uk/adviceandwelfare/pets/rodents/degus/environment
- https://www.rspca.org.uk/adviceandwelfare/pets/rodents/degus/diet
- https://www.rspca.org.uk/adviceandwelfare/pets/rodents/degus/health
- https://www.rspca.org.uk/adviceandwelfare/pets/rodents/degus/company
- https://www.rspca.org.uk/adviceandwelfare/pets/rodents/degus/behaviour
- https://pdsa.org.uk/pet-help-and-advice/looking-after-your-pet/small-pets/ideal-environment-for-degus
- https://www.petmd.com/exotic/care/caring-for-a-degu

## Чим годувати хомʼяка: що можна, а що не можна

URL: https://roddihealth.app/blog/khomiaky/chym-goduvaty-khomiaka
Updated: 2026-11-16

Summary: Більшу частину раціону хомʼяка має становити гранульований корм для хомʼяків. Свіже дають помірно, бо його надлишок може спричинити діарею, а для хомʼяка вона небезпечна: він швидко втрачає рідину.


### Що має бути основою

Основа — гранульований корм для хомʼяків. PDSA пояснює, що всі гранули однакові, тож хомʼяк не може вибрати лише смачне, а суміші на кшталт мюслі радить не давати як єдиний корм. PetMD рекомендує корм із вмістом білка 15–25% і приблизно столову ложку їжі на день, залежно від виду.

Свіжі овочі обирайте з високим вмістом клітковини й давайте потроху: PDSA називає одну-дві чайні ложки свіжого на день. Хомʼяки активні вночі, тож свіже зручно давати ввечері. Фрукти містять багато цукру. Для сирійських PetMD радить давати яблуко чи ягоди лише зрідка й крихітними порціями, для карликових — чайну ложку фруктів один-три рази на тиждень. PDSA попереджає, що російські карликові хомʼяки схильні до діабету, тож солодкого їм варто давати особливо мало.


### Чи можна хомʼяку: коротка таблиця

ПродуктВідповідьПриміткаВиноград, ревіньНіRSPCA: можуть бути отруйними для гризунівЧасникНіPetMDЦибуляКраще не даватиPetMD радить уникати, а PDSA має її в списку дозволених. Безпечніше не даватиШоколад, кава, алкогольНіPetMD: токсичніЦитрусовіНіPetMD радить уникати; PDSA вважає, що поки краще не даватиМигдальНіУ переліку PetMD; PDSA допускає інші горіхи як рідкісні ласощіСирі боби, сира картопляНіPetMDПомідориОбережноPetMD радить уникати незрілих, PDSA допускає помідорКісточки й насіння фруктівНіЗокрема насіння яблукСолодке, солоне, червоне мʼясоНіPetMDЯблуко без насіння, банан, персикПомірноМаленький шматочок; PDSA має їх у списку дозволенихКабачок, болгарський перець, моркваПомірноКабачок і перець у списку PDSA, моркву згадує PetMD


### Чого остерігатися
- Різкої зміни корму чи марки: RSPCA, PDSA і PetMD попереджають, що це може засмутити кишечник і спричинити діарею.
- Надлишку овочів, фруктів чи солодких ласощів.
- Зіпсованих залишків. Хомʼяки ховають їжу про запас, тож свіже швидко псується в схованках. PetMD радить прибирати залишки й заховане свіже щодня, а для сирійських — через кілька годин.


### Вода

Свіжа чиста вода має бути завжди. RSPCA радить поїлку-трубочку без кульки, бо з кулькового клапана хомʼяку важко пити. PetMD радить міняти воду щодня й перевіряти, чи поїлка не протікає й не погризена.
